subject: maths
pattern: Inverse Trigonometric Functions carries about 6-8 marks in the Karnataka 2nd PUC paper: a 1-mark principal value, a 2-mark domain/range or identity proof, a 3-mark simplification or proof, and a 5-mark proof involving sum of inverse tangents. Examiners expect the principal value branches to be quoted correctly and the substitution step (x = tan theta etc.) to be shown with the range check.

questions.answer: Let $\sin^{-1}(-\tfrac12)=y$, so $\sin y=-\tfrac12=\sin\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ with $y\in[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}]$. Hence the principal value is $-\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
Let $\cos^{-1}(-\tfrac12)=y$, so $\cos y=-\tfrac12=\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$ with $y\in[0,\pi]$. Hence the principal value is $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

questions.q: Write the domain and the range (principal value branch) of $\cos^{-1}x$ and $\tan^{-1}x$.
questions.answer: $\cos^{-1}x$: domain $[-1,1]$, range (principal value branch) $[0,\pi]$. $\tan^{-1}x$: domain $\mathbb{R}$, range (principal value branch) $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

Let $\sin^{-1}(-x)=y$. Then $\sin y=-x$, so $x=-\sin y=\sin(-y)$. Therefore $\sin^{-1}x=-y$ (as $-y$ lies in $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}]$), i.e. $y=-\sin^{-1}x$. Hence $\sin^{-1}(-x)=-\sin^{-1}x$.

$\sin^{-1}(\sin x)=x$ only if $x\in[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}]$. Here $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ is outside, so write $\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=\sin\left(\pi-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. Hence $\sin^{-1}\left(\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Let $x=\tan\theta$, so $\theta=\tan^{-1}x$. Since $|x|\le1$, $\theta\in\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$. Then $\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}=\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}=\sin2\theta$ with $2\theta\in\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. Hence $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}=\sin^{-1}(\sin2\theta)=2\theta=2\tan^{-1}x$.

Let $x=\sin\theta$, so $\theta=\sin^{-1}x$. For $x\in[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$, $\theta\in\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right]$ and $3\theta\in\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. Now $3x-4x^3=3\sin\theta-4\sin^3\theta=\sin3\theta$. Therefore $\sin^{-1}(3x-4x^3)=\sin^{-1}(\sin3\theta)=3\theta=3\sin^{-1}x$.

Put $x=\tan\theta$, so $\theta=\tan^{-1}x$. Then $\dfrac{\sqrt{1+\tan^2\theta}-1}{\tan\theta}=\dfrac{\sec\theta-1}{\tan\theta}=\dfrac{1-\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=\dfrac{2\sin^2(\theta/2)}{2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)}=\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}$. Hence the expression $=\tan^{-1}\left(\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)=\dfrac{\theta}{2}=\dfrac12\tan^{-1}x$.

Let $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{12}{13}=\alpha$ so $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{12}{5}$; $\cos^{-1}\dfrac45=\beta$ so $\tan\beta=\dfrac34$. Then $\tan(\alpha+\beta)=\dfrac{\tfrac{12}{5}+\tfrac34}{1-\tfrac{12}{5}\cdot\tfrac34}=\dfrac{63/20}{-4/5}=-\dfrac{63}{16}$. Since $\alpha,\beta$ are acute with $\tan\alpha\tan\beta>1$, $\alpha+\beta$ lies in $(\tfrac{\pi}{2},\pi)$, so $\alpha+\beta=\pi-\tan^{-1}\dfrac{63}{16}$. Hence $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{12}{13}+\cos^{-1}\dfrac45+\tan^{-1}\dfrac{63}{16}=\pi$.

Use $2\tan^{-1}x=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1-x^2}$ for $|x|<1$. $2\tan^{-1}\tfrac12=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{1-\tfrac14}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac43$. Then $\tan^{-1}\tfrac43+\tan^{-1}\tfrac17$: here $\tfrac43\cdot\tfrac17=\tfrac4{21}<1$, so the sum is $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\tfrac43+\tfrac17}{1-\tfrac{4}{21}}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{31/21}{17/21}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{31}{17}$. Hence proved.
